summary: Contract Year 2028 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, and Medicare Cost Plan Program (CMS-4214-P2) Background On November 20, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a proposed rule that is intended to revise the Medicare Advantage (MA) Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program (Part D), and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) Program. The Contract Year (CY) 2028 MA and Part D proposed rule aims to revitalize competition in MA and Part D and give beneficiaries more meaningful choices in how they receive care. If finalized, the proposed policy updates, alongside a new CMS Innovation Center (CMMI) model, would break down administrative barriers for new market entrants and pioneer localized care innovations. This is the second rule proposing changes applicable to CY 2028. The first rule, proposing changes to implement sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 ( CMS-4214-P ), was issued on October 16, 2026. Establishing a Standardized Definition of “Healthy Food” for MA Supplemental Benefits CMS proposes to establish a clear “healthy food” standard that is aligned with the 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans and apply it to all supplemental benefit categories that include food. Under this proposal, food items must either meet the CMS-defined standard or be specifically recommended by a healthcare provider to meet an enrollee’s medical needs. For example, items like certain high-caloric oral nutrient supplements could still be covered if specifically recommended by a health care provider to meet an enrollee's medical needs. Aligning Data and Value to Nurture Competition and Efficiency in Medicare Advantage (ADVaNCE MA) Model CMS is proposing the CMS Innovation Center’s first mandatory MA model. The model aims to spur local plan competition, enhance beneficiary choice and value, reduce Medicare expenditures, improve quality, and protect taxpayers. If finalized, the 10-year model test would begin in CY 2029, with a pre-implementation period starting on June 8, 2027, operating in randomly selected states with participation from a variety of plan types. The components of the ADVaNCE MA model are: CMMI Inferred Risk Adjustment Model: Explore, through shadow testing, an innovative risk adjustment methodology that builds upon the current CMS Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk adjustment model by integrating multiple, existing data sources already available to CMS, including Original Medicare (OM) claims data, MA encounter data, and enrollment data. This shadow test would compile information on the usability of an alternative approach that could offer greater payment accuracy compared to the traditional risk adjustment methodology while not disrupting the MA market. The learnings from the shadow test are expected to inform future risk adjustment policy. The Diamond Ratings System: A redesigned quality program implemented in select states would replace the current MA and Part D Star Ratings and Quality Bonus Payment system with a localized, cohort-based, quality framework to incentivize continuous improvement and enable beneficiaries to make meaningful, geographically relevant plan comparisons in their local areas. Targeted Supplemental Benefits for Low-Income Subsidy (LIS)-Eligible Individuals: New regulatory flexibilities would allow MA organizations to offer/target to Part D LIS-eligible individuals certain supplemental benefits, some of which are currently only available to chronically ill beneficiaries through Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill. These supplemental benefits – healthy food and produce, transportation for non-medical needs, and supports for caregivers – have a focus on high-value prevention and serious illness support, with the goal of improving quality outcomes and reducing Medicare expenditures by avoiding and delaying costly, downstream care. Dialysis Carveout for Beneficiaries with End-Stage Renal Disease: CMS is considering, but not currently proposing, to exclude payment for dialysis services from MA for beneficiaries with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) as a component of the ADVaNCE MA Model. Under this carveout, for beneficiaries with ESRD, dialysis would be covered by OM and paid through the ESRD Prospective Payment System (PPS), while the beneficiaries’ MA organizations would remain financially responsible for all other covered services. If proposed as a future component of the ADVaNCE MA model, details regarding interactions under the ESRD PPS would be included in future rulemaking. Strengthening Current Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Policies Using a CMS Approval Mechanism for Use of the Disaster/Emergency Special Enrollment Period (SEP) and Other Technical Changes: To provide proper oversight of the disaster/emergency SEP, CMS is proposing to require beneficiaries to obtain prior approval through 1-800-MEDICARE. This measure is intended to promote appropriate use of the SEP and reduce the risk of fraud and abuse. Data regarding the use of MA and Part D SEPs suggest that plans may be misusing the disaster/emergency SEP to enroll beneficiaries who were not affected by a declared disaster or emergency, or whose ability to make an MA or Part D election could not reasonably have been affected by such an event. The proposed requirement would help prevent plans, agents, and brokers from directing beneficiaries to use the disaster or emergency SEP when they are not eligible. Cost Sharing Standards for Ground Ambulance and Emergency Services : CMS proposes new dollar limits for ground ambulance and emergency service cost-sharing, based on the latest OM data. Current limits rely on 2021 figures, and CMS has never set a specific cost-sharing dollar cap for ground ambulance services. CMS would update the emergency services cost-sharing limit to $180–$240 (range based on the plan’s maximum out-of-pocket (MOOP) amount), reflecting current OM cost projections. CMS would also cap ground ambulance services coinsurance at 30–50% of the Medicare average cost, translating to a $180–$300 limit (range also based on the plan’s MOOP amount). This would give ground ambulance services a defined dollar cap, with the $300 limit for a lower MOOP limit matching the existing 50% coinsurance standard used for this service (currently for all MOOP types). If finalized, going forward, CMS would update the ground ambulance and emergency services limits every year using the latest projections from the CMS Office of the Actuary (OACT). This is consistent with how CMS already updates copayment limits annually for other service categories, like professional services, to keep cost-sharing limits current. Enrollment Capacity Limits : CMS is proposing to formalize the requirements for MA plans to submit a request for an enrollment capacity limit by establishing requirements for evaluating an enrollment capacity request as part of the bid submission process. CMS is also proposing to rescind the regulation that allows MA plans to request an enrollment capacity limit outside the bid submission process to eliminate gaming opportunities. Finally, CMS proposes to establish a SEP for enrollees who select a plan that is at its enrollment capacity and miss the opportunity to elect a different MA plan. This would ensure that enrollees are still able to select a plan, even if their first choice may not be available. Use of Existing Interoperability Application Programming Interface (APIs) for Prior Authorization Transactions : CMS proposes to establish a requirement that MA organization contracts with providers must include a term requiring in-network providers to submit prior authorization requests and associated documentation through the plan’s FHIR-based Prior Authorization API. CMS would also require MA organizations to test and confirm the ability of their in-network providers to send and receive information through the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API annually. The proposal also includes a Request for Information (RFI) regarding potential implications for rural and other health care providers, as well as an RFI regarding options for further advancing the health tech ecosystem. Enrollee Notification Requirements for Provider Terminations, Continuity of Care, and SEP Notice Consolidation : CMS proposes to define a "significant change" to an MA plan's provider network and require plans to notify enrollees when the significant change is final. A network change would be significant if the provider termination meets either of two thresholds: the termination affects at least 10% of the plan's enrolled population, or the terminated provider represents at least 10% of the plan's contracted network for a given specialty. When a significant change occurs, affected enrollees would be informed by their MA plan that they are eligible for a SEP. CMS also proposes revising the definition of "affected enrollee" at 42 CFR § 422.62(b)(23)(ii) to align with 42 CFR § 422.111(e), applying a consistent one-year lookback period regardless of provider type. Under this standard, any enrollee who saw the terminated provider within the year before termination—and whose plan meets the 10% significance threshold—qualifies for notification and the SEP. Finally, CMS proposes a new continuity-of-care requirement: MA plans must continue covering services furnished by terminated providers to affected enrollees at in-network rates with in-network cost sharing for at least 90 days following a provider termination. Seamless Continuation of Coverage for Newly Medicare-Eligible Individuals: To streamline the enrollment process into an MA plan for individuals currently enrolled in Marketplace or commercial plans who are approaching Medicare eligibility, CMS is considering creating a seamless continuation of coverage process, similar to what existed prior to 2018, where certain newly Medicare-eligible individuals could be automatically enrolled in an MA plan offered by the same organization that the individual chose for their current non-Medicare coverage. This would improve the transition into Medicare by automatically placing newly eligible beneficiaries into coverage that more closely aligns with their health insurance experience prior to Medicare eligibility, while maintaining their ability to choose whatever Medicare coverage option works best for them. Transforming Agent and Broker Compensation and Oversight CMS is proposing several changes to reduce burden, add guardrails, streamline regulations, and provide a more flexible framework for agent and broker compensation and oversight. Specifically, CMS is proposing to: Eliminate CMS defined compensation caps and renewal limits for agent and broker compensation; Streamline agent and broker oversight with market-based compensation guardrails, Eliminate duplicative reporting and training requirements, Eliminate referral fee caps; Revise and clarify definitions; Enhance compensation data collection to increase transparency; Create a methodology to identify compensation outliers with restrictions around payment of outlier amounts; Permit organizations to change compensation amounts during the plan year, with advance notification to CMS; Remove unneeded or overly prescriptive regulatory requirements. Strengthening Maximum Fair Price Effectuation Policies for Medicare Advantage CMS is proposing policies to facilitate the effectuation of the maximum fair price (MFP) under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program for selected drugs payable under Part B that are furnished or administered to an individual enrolled in MA.
